newsitem.title: SWEDEN: Sweden PM seen ducking EMU decision to save skin.
newsitem.headline: Sweden PM seen ducking EMU decision to save skin.

text.p: Swedish Prime Minister Goran Persson is likely to postpone joining Europe's economic and monetary union (EMU) until after its start in 1999 to avoid a political backlash that could lead to his downfall, analysts say.

Persson, described as a pragmatic politician, is not likely to risk losing both face and position by giving an early EMU entrance the nod while anti-EMU sentiment prevails in his ruling Social Democratic party.
"It would be political suicide for Persson to say yes to EMU," Knut Hallberg, senior economist at Swedbank, told Reuters.
Hallberg referred to polls showing both that Swedes have a fairly hostile attitude to EMU and that voters stung by harsh budget cutbacks have fled the Social Democrats.

A poll published on Thursday showed 30 percent of Social Democrats opposed an EMU link, while 42 percent wanted to wait and see for a couple of years after 1999. Only 13 percent wanted to join in the first round and 15 percent were uncertain.
Among Swedes in general the poll showed around 30 percent of the population were against EMU while 35 percent wanted to wait and see.
Support for the Social Democrats has fallen to 27.6 percent from 45 percent at the time of the 1994 general elections, according to an April poll.
Persson's position as prime minister is far from rock solid as he does not enjoy the solid support in his own party that predecessors Ingvar Carlsson and Olof Palme enjoyed.
What is more, his overbearing attitude towards party colleagues and rivals has put many people off, Hallberg said.
To avoid rocking the boat, Persson is expected to delay a decision on EMU membership to sometime after 1999.

"Persson wants to push the EMU issue aside so the party can show a united front at the 1998 general elections and at the party congress in September (this year) which will be the beginning of the election campaign," Carl B Hamilton, chief economist at Handelsbanken, said.
Aslong as Persson decides to play a wait-and-see game on EMU, the path will be fairly smooth toward a formal Swedish decision along those lines.
Firstly the Social Democratic party's executive committee will announce its view sometime in May or June.

Then the party's leadership will issue a recommendation -- which is almost sure to coincide with the committee's opinion -- to a September party congress that will decide the Social Democrats official EMU view.
After the congress, the The Social Democratic minority government could put a proposal to parliament and parliament could rule on EMU sometime in early 1998.

A wait-and-see attitude may be supported by the Centre Party, the minority government's informal cooperation partner, which at the moment opposes EMU and is calling for a referendum, or possibly extra parliamentary elections.
